the ways in which the social identities and communicative practices of older people are constructed and reproduced through talk and interaction, and how this process can be influenced by young people.
how young people and older people talk to each other and how these conversations can contribute to the reproduction of negative attitudes toward aging and to successful aging.
how young and old people communicate with one another, and with how these communication patterns are implicated in the construction of age identities and in the reproduction or reduction of ageism.

the way we talk to older people is not only problematic, but it can also be improved through a variety of means.
young and old people do not communicate well with each other.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the intergenerational talk and communication between young and old people is a complex, dynamic, and potentially productive social interaction that is often shaped by ageism and stereotypes.
the communication patterns we observe are not conducive to intergenerational harmony and that we need to find better ways to facilitate intergenerational dialogue.

the intergenerational communication of older people is a complex and multidimensional process that is not well understood, and that more research is needed in order to understand the ways in which young and old people communicate and how such communication can be improved.
The main takeaway from our work is that
intergenerational communication should be approached as a social justice and public health issue.
the way we talk to each other matters, and that the ways we communicate with older people can either help or hinder successful aging and intergenerational relationships.
intergenerational communication is not only about how older people are treated, but also about how young people treat and communicate with them.
